notes.title: Look at the building
notes.fact: Architectural works, sculpture and inscriptions can form part of cultural heritage.
notes.connection: Notice the temple-inspired gateways and carved surfaces. This environment is fictional, not a surveyed reconstruction.

notes.title: Repair needs knowledge
notes.fact: Unsuitable repairs can damage ceramics. Real pottery repair requires knowledge of the material and suitable techniques.
notes.connection: Joining the game's pot fragments is a simplified observation puzzle. It is not a guide to repairing real objects.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Care of Ceramics and Glass, Notes 5/1

notes.title: Keep a record
notes.fact: A professional inventory helps protect museum collections and prevent illicit trafficking.
notes.connection: Compare the vault ledger and the objects you recover. Recording what belongs in a collection matters.
notes.source: UNESCO, Museums and Collections Recommendation (2015), paragraph 8

notes.title: Water changes materials
notes.fact: Excavated objects can change after removal from the ground; salts and environmental conditions can damage archaeological materials.
notes.connection: The stepwell uses water as a game mechanism. Real excavated objects need specialist care, not a quick rinse.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Caring for archaeological collections

notes.title: Seeing and preserving
notes.fact: Light helps us see collections, but it can fade sensitive colours. Both brightness and exposure time matter.
notes.connection: The Sun Wall lets you observe light paths. Its mechanism is fictional; museum lighting also considers protection.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Agent of Deterioration: Light, Ultraviolet and Infrared

notes.title: Pass heritage forward
notes.fact: Museums support education and cultural transmission, and citizens share responsibility for caring for heritage.
notes.connection: Return the fictional objects to their community. The recovery story is an invented adventure, not a historical event.
notes.source: UNESCO, Museums and Collections Recommendation (2015), paragraph 2

notes.title: Craft is also knowledge
notes.fact: Traditional craftsmanship includes the skills and knowledge used to make objects, not just the finished products.
notes.connection: The fictional market places dyers, potters and brass workers beside their tools. Observe the people and processes as well as the goods.

notes.title: Skills pass between people
notes.fact: Living heritage depends on people passing knowledge and skills from person to person and between generations.
notes.connection: Tea-lane neighbours share a working space. This invented market illustrates a living community rather than a collection of treasures.

notes.title: Mangal Aarti and the temple beginnings
notes.fact: At Puri in Odisha, the present Shree Jagannath Temple began under King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty in the twelfth century. This bell and conch recall Mangal Aarti, the early morning worship of Jagannath. Their sound calls attention to prayer and the daily service that keeps the temple tradition alive. Temple tradition also tells of King Indradyumna and sacred timber. That is a cherished foundation legend, distinct from the documented history of the present stone temple.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.

notes.title: Palm-leaf writing and Gita Govinda
notes.fact: This palm-leaf manuscript recalls tala patra, an Odisha craft that preserves writing and pictures on prepared palm leaves. Artists incise fine lines with a stylus and darken them with pigment. The Gita Govinda was composed by the twelfth-century poet Jayadeva. Its devotional verses are sung in Jagannath worship, connecting poetry, music and temple service. Preserving a manuscript protects more than words. It keeps a language, an artist's skill and generations of community memory available to the people who come after us.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.

notes.title: Nilachakra and Pattachitra craftsmanship
notes.fact: The Nilachakra is the sacred wheel above the Shree Jagannath Temple at Puri. It is made from ashtadhatu, an alloy traditionally described as eight metals. The temple flag is associated with this wheel. The small seal you recovered recalls that landmark; the actual sacred wheel remains on the temple. Pattachitra is Odisha's detailed story-painting tradition. Artists use careful outlines and prepared colours to preserve devotional stories, including stories associated with Jagannath.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.

notes.title: Mahaprasad and water traditions
notes.fact: This vessel introduces Mahaprasad, the sacred food offered at Shree Jagannath Temple. The temple kitchen prepares offerings in earthen pots through the skilled service of its cooks. Rohini Kunda is a sacred water place within the temple tradition. A water vessel can help us remember the place of water, offerings and daily care in worship. Nirmalya includes dried sacred rice cherished by devotees. Food traditions remind us that heritage lives through people who prepare, share and care for it, as well as through buildings.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.

notes.title: Ratha Yatra and the chariot makers
notes.fact: Ratha Yatra is the great chariot festival of Puri. Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra travel along Bada Danda, the Grand Avenue, towards Gundicha Temple. Jagannath's chariot is Nandighosha, with sixteen wheels. Balabhadra's is Taladhwaja and Subhadra's is Darpadalana. Each chariot has its own established design. Skilled carpenters build the chariots anew each year. The wheel and banner recall a living tradition in which making, devotion and community participation carry knowledge forward.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.

notes.title: Living heritage and Nabakalebara
notes.fact: A kalasha is a crowning vessel form in temple architecture. This finial ornament helps us notice how the upper parts of a temple contribute to its identity and craftsmanship. At Puri, Nabakalebara is the periodic renewal of the sacred wooden images in the Jagannath tradition. The images are associated with sacred neem wood, or daru. This is why heritage is more than the price of wood or metal. People preserve and renew its meaning through knowledge, care and worship. Protecting heritage means protecting living community memory.
notes.connection: Fictional teaching replicas; sacred images and authentic temple objects remain untouched.
